In mathematics, and particularly [[functional analysis]], the '''Helly space''', named after [[Eduard Helly]], consists of all [[monotonically increasing]] [[function (mathematics)|function]]s {{nowrap|1=ƒ : [0,1] → [0,1]}}, where [0,1] denotes the [[closed interval]] given by the [[set (mathematics)|set]] of all ''x'' such that {{nowrap|1=0 ≤ ''x'' ≤ 1.}}<ref name="CEIT1">{{Citation|first1=L. A.|last1=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|publisher=Dover|year=1995|pages=127 − 128|isbn=0-486-68735-X}}</ref> In other words, for all {{nowrap|1=0 ≤ ''x'' ≤ 1}} we have {{nowrap|1=0 ≤ ƒ(''x'') ≤ 1}} and also if {{nowrap|1=''x'' ≤ ''y''}} then {{nowrap|1=ƒ(''x'') ≤ ƒ(''y'').}}

Let the closed interval [0,1] be denoted simply by ''I''. We can form the space ''I<sup>I</sup>'' by taking the [[uncountable]] [[Cartesian product]] of closed intervals:<ref name="CEIT2">{{Citation|first1=L. A.|last1=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|publisher=Dover|year=1995|page=125 − 126|isbn=0-486-68735-X}}</ref>
:<math> I^I = \prod_{i \in I} I_i </math>
The space ''I<sup>I</sup>'' is exactly the space of functions {{nowrap|1=ƒ : [0,1] → [0,1]}}. For each point ''x'' in [0,1] we assign the point ƒ(''x'') in {{nowrap|1=''I<sub>x</sub>'' = [0,1].}}<ref>{{Cite book|first=R|last=Penrose|title=The Road to Reality: A Complete guide to the Laws of the Universe|publisher=Vintage Books|year=2005|pages=368 − 369|isbn=0-09-944068-7}}</ref>

Helly's space is [[Convex set|convex]] as a subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^{[0,1]}</math>.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1902.03235 |author1=Justin Tatch Moore |title=The method of forcing |date=2019 |class=math.LO }}</ref>

== Topology ==

The Helly space is a subset of ''I<sup>I</sup>''. The space ''I<sup>I</sup>'' has its own topology, namely the [[product topology]].<ref name="CEIT2"/> The Helly space has a topology; namely the [[induced topology]] as a subset of ''I<sup>I</sup>''.<ref name="CEIT1"/> It is [[normal space|normal Haudsdorff]], [[compact space|compact]], [[separable space|separable]], and [[first-countable space|first-countable]] but not [[second-countable space|second-countable]].
